summary: Find and verify papers/benchmarks related to the chart cue-conflict experiment

result.title: Multimodal Neurons in Artificial Neural Networks
result.authors: Gabriel Goh, Nick Cammarata, Chelsea Voss, Shan Carter, Michael Petrov, Ludwig Schubert, Alec Radford, Chris Olah
result.key_finding: CLIP contains multimodal neurons that fire for the same concept whether it appears as a photo, a drawing, or the written word, and because they react so strongly to text, handwritten mislabels on real objects ("typographic attacks") often flip CLIP's classification (a Granny Smith apple labelled "iPod" was read as iPod with 99.7% zero-shot probability), while pasting class-name text onto ImageNet validation images reached up to about 97% attack success with roughly 7% of pixels changed.
result.what_it_measures: How CLIP's neurons respond to the same concept shown as a photo, a symbol or written text, and whether text placed in the image can steer the classifier.
result.relevance: background (origin of the 'model reads the label instead of looking at the object' idea; our conflict condition is a typographic attack aimed at chart marks instead of objects)
result.notes:
Checked against the live Distill page and its article bundle (index.bundle.js, which holds the body text and figure data). Metadata is correct: published March 4, 2021, DOI 10.23915/distill.00030, all eight authors in the order given. Distill is a peer-reviewed journal, so "Distill" is the right venue.

The candidate's key finding is right in substance with one overstatement. The attack is literally done by handwriting ("simply using handwriting?"), and the apple/iPod example is real. In the figure data for the apple-with-"iPod" image (in_the_wild_round_2-apple-ipod.png), zero-shot gives iPod 0.9968 and Granny Smith 0.0013. But "classify the object as whatever the label says" goes too far. The article says these attacks "often change the image's classification," and the Figure 14 caption says some attacks work better than others and some objects resist. The same apple/iPod image under the linear probe still leans Granny Smith (0.161 vs iPod 0.010). So the 99.7% number is a zero-shot result, not a universal one. The model in the physical-attack figure is CLIP RN50-4x.

Two more details for the blog:
1. There is an automated ImageNet-validation evaluation: up to 97% attack success with about 7% of pixels changed, which the authors call competitive with Adversarial Patch. Attack words were found by looking at neurons (piggy bank, waste container, Siamese cat) or by brute-force search over class names (rifle, pizza, radio, iPod, shark, library).
2. A "Comparison with the Stroop Effect" section has CLIP classify the ink color of words that name a different color. It errs heavily, much as humans slow down and make mistakes on incongruent labels. This is arguably closer to the chart-conflict condition (written number vs drawn mark) than the apple example.

The relevance tag "background / origin of the reads-the-label idea" fits. This is a Distill interpretability article, not a benchmark.

result.title: Unveiling Typographic Deceptions: Insights of the Typographic Vulnerability in Large Vision-Language Models
result.authors: Hao Cheng, Erjia Xiao, Jindong Gu, Le Yang, Jinhao Duan, Jize Zhang, Jiahang Cao, Kaidi Xu, Renjing Xu
result.key_finding: Typographic attacks, already known to fool CLIP-style VLMs, are shown to be a widespread threat to well-known commercial and open-source LVLMs; the authors evaluate them on a new large Typographic Dataset covering several multimodal tasks and text factors, derive three findings about why the attacks work, and while validating those findings reduce the attack-induced performance drop from 42.07% to 13.90%.
result.what_it_measures: How much misleading text written into an image hurts commercial and open-source LVLMs across several multimodal tasks, using a large typographic attack dataset with varied text properties.
result.relevance: partial overlap (misleading text inside the image, as in ours, but on natural photos and object/attribute questions, not chart values)
result.notes: Checked the arXiv abstract page (v1 29 Feb 2024, v3 19 Sep 2024; the comment says "accepted by ECCV 2024") and the official ECVA/ECCV 2024 proceedings page (ecva.net, paper 7650). First author Hao Cheng is correct, and so are the year, venue and URL. Title: the arXiv version ends in the singular "Large Vision-Language Model", while the ECCV proceedings use the plural "Models". The candidate title matches the ECCV version, so I kept it. The candidate key finding is faithful. One small nuance: the abstract says the drop from 42.07% to 13.90% came out of validating the three findings, not from a separately proposed defense method. Code and dataset: github.com/ChaduCheng/TypoDecep. Relevance note for the user: this is a benchmark of misleading text overlaid on natural images across multimodal tasks. It does not cover chart values or numbers that conflict with plotted marks.

result.title: SCAM: A Real-World Typographic Robustness Evaluation for Multimodal Foundation Models
result.authors: Justus Westerhoff, Erblina Purelku, Jakob Hackstein, Jonas Loos, Leo Pinetzki, Erik Rodner, Lorenz Hufe
result.venue: CVPR 2025 Workshop (EVAL-FoMo-2); also published in Journal of Data-centric Machine Learning Research (DMLR), 2026
result.key_finding: On SCAM (1,162 real photos with misleading handwritten words), typographic attacks still significantly degrade state-of-the-art LVLMs, especially those whose vision encoders are inherently vulnerable; larger LLM backbones reduce this vulnerability and improve typographic understanding, and synthetic attacks closely resemble real handwritten ones.
result.what_it_measures: Accuracy of VLMs and LVLMs on 1,162 real photos of objects with a misleading handwritten word, plus a clean set (NoSCAM) and a synthetic-text set (SynthSCAM).
result.relevance: partial overlap (clean / attacked / synthetic triplet is close to our consistent / conflict design; their result that a bigger LLM resists more is a useful comparison for 3B PaliGemma 2 at 224 vs 448)
result.notes: I checked the arXiv API record (v7, 18 Mar 2026) and the project page. Every metadata field matches. The first author is Justus Westerhoff, out of 7 authors. v1 went up on 2025-04-07. The arXiv comment says "Accepted at CVPR 2025 Workshop EVAL-FoMo-2" and the journal ref says "Journal of Data-centric Machine Learning Research (2026)". The project page also lists it as published at DMLR via OpenReview, so the candidate's venue is correct. The candidate key finding is faithful to the abstract. My rewrite only adds two things from the abstract: the drop in performance is "significant", and larger LLM backbones also improve typographic understanding. The abstract also says training data and model architecture affect how vulnerable a model is. The abstract does not name NoSCAM or SynthSCAM, but the project page (bliss-e-v.github.io/SCAM-project-page) confirms both: SCAM is real handwritten attacks, SynthSCAM is digital text added to the images, and NoSCAM is the same images with the attack removed. So the what_it_measures field is accurate. Relevance caveat: SCAM tests object classification with a misleading word, not charts or numbers, so the overlap with the chart-conflict design is only partial.

result.title: Words or Vision: Do Vision-Language Models Have Blind Faith in Text?
result.authors: Ailin Deng, Tri Cao, Zhirui Chen, Bryan Hooi
result.key_finding: Across ten VLMs and four vision-centric tasks with altered text, the models trust the text far more than the image when the two disagree ("blind faith in text"), so performance drops sharply when the text is corrupted; a larger language model reduces this only slightly, token order can make it worse through positional biases carried over from the LLM, and supervised fine-tuning with text augmentation reduces it.
result.what_it_measures: How 10 VLMs behave on four vision-centric tasks when the accompanying text is changed so it contradicts the image, and how instructions, LLM size, text relevance, token order and modality certainty change this.
result.relevance: same question (marks vs text, which wins), but their conflicting text is given next to the image in the prompt, while ours is printed inside the chart pixels
result.notes: Checked on the arXiv abstract page (2503.02199, submitted 4 Mar 2025). The comments field says "Accepted to CVPR 2025". All candidate fields are correct: title, first author Ailin Deng (co-authors Tri Cao, Zhirui Chen, Bryan Hooi), year, venue and URL. The candidate key finding matches the abstract. The abstract also lists two points the candidate leaves out: (1) the factors studied include the interplay between visual and textual certainty, as well as instruction prompts, LLM size, text relevance and token order; (2) a theoretical analysis suggests the bias may come from an imbalance between pure-text and multimodal data in training. I did not find a CVF open-access page in search. The arXiv comment and CVPR listings are enough to confirm the venue. Relevance note is fair: in this paper the conflicting text is given in the prompt next to the image, not printed inside the image.

result.title: Mixed Signals: Decoding VLMs' Reasoning and Underlying Bias in Vision-Language Conflict
result.authors: Pouya Pezeshkpour, Moin Aminnaseri, Estevam Hruschka
result.key_finding: On five datasets of mismatched image-text pairs (math, science, visual descriptions), VLMs favour the text on simpler queries and shift toward the image as queries get more complex; the bias correlates with model scale, and the image-minus-text preference gap runs from +56.8% (image favoured) to -85.1% (text favoured) depending on task and model, while the three mitigations (simple prompt changes, explicit conflict-handling instructions, and per-modality task decomposition) vary widely in effect, tied to the model's overall task performance and the modality involved.
result.what_it_measures: Which modality VLMs follow on five datasets of deliberately mismatched image-text pairs (math, science, visual description), scored as image-preferred vs text-preferred answers, plus three mitigation prompts.
result.relevance: same question (an image-vs-text preference score like our 'follows marks vs follows text' rate); the conflicting text is in the prompt, not rendered in the image
result.notes: I checked the ACL Anthology page (Findings of EMNLP 2025, pp. 24833-24848) and arXiv 2504.08974. The title, first author, year, venue and URL in the candidate are all correct. The full author list is Pezeshkpour, Aminnaseri and Hruschka, all at Megagon Labs. The candidate key finding is faithful but leaves two things out. First, the abstract says mitigation effectiveness depends on base task performance and also on the specific modality. Second, not all three mitigations are prompts: the third is a task decomposition strategy that analyses each modality separately before combining them. The ranges differ between versions. The ACL camera-ready abstract gives +56.8% to -85.1%, while arXiv v1 (11 Apr 2025, the only version) gives -74.4%, so cite the ACL figure. The dataset and code are released.

result.title: Evaluating and Steering Modality Preferences in Multi-modal LLMs (ICML 2026 title; arXiv title: "Evaluating and Steering Modality Preferences in Multimodal Large Language Model")
result.authors: Yu Zhang, Jinlong Ma, Yongshuai Hou, Xuefeng Bai, Kehai Chen, Yang Xiang, Jun Yu, Min Zhang
result.key_finding: On the MC² benchmark of controlled evidence conflicts, all 20 tested MLLMs show a clear modality preference that is statistically associated with their downstream performance; the preference can be changed by instructions and read from latent representations, and a representation-engineering probe-and-steer method controls it without fine-tuning and improves several multimodal understanding and reasoning tasks.
result.what_it_measures: Modality preference of 20 MLLMs on the MC² benchmark, which sets up controlled conflicts between visual and textual evidence; also probes the preference in hidden representations and steers it.
result.relevance: same question (a benchmark built to measure modality preference under conflict); text is a separate input, not printed in the image
result.notes: Checked the arXiv abstract page (v1 to v3) and the ICML 2026 poster page (icml.cc/virtual/2026/poster/61222). The paper exists. The ICML 2026 poster acceptance is confirmed, the authors are right and Yu Zhang is the first author, and the URL is correct. The two titles differ slightly, as the candidate already noted. One part of the candidate claim is wrong: no version of the abstract says the preference usually goes toward text. Only the lay summary on the ICML page says that, in the words "often text, even when the image is important". So if the blog says models lean toward text, credit the lay summary or the paper body, not the abstract. Everything else in the claim matches the abstract. Version differences: v1 tested 18 MLLMs and named hallucination mitigation and multimodal machine translation as the downstream uses. v3 and the ICML version test 20 MLLMs and add that the preference is linked to downstream performance. Relevance to the current experiment: MC² puts the conflicting text in the prompt as a separate input, not printed inside the image, so it is a close cousin of the chart cue-conflict setup rather than the same design.

result.title: Are Large Vision Language Models up to the Challenge of Chart Comprehension and Reasoning? An Extensive Investigation into the Capabilities and Limitations of LVLMs
result.authors: Mohammed Saidul Islam, Raian Rahman, Ahmed Masry, Md Tahmid Rahman Laskar, Mir Tafseer Nayeem, Enamul Hoque
result.key_finding: In a broad evaluation of closed and open-source LVLMs on chart QA, summarization and fact-checking tasks, the models write fluent text that captures high-level data insights but also hallucinate, make factual errors and show data bias.
result.what_it_measures: GPT-4V and Gemini on chart QA, summarization and fact-checking; includes ChartQA*, a version of ChartQA with the printed data-value labels removed (checked in the paper body, not the abstract).
result.relevance: partial overlap (ChartQA* matches our no-numbers condition and shows that models lean on printed numbers; it has no conflict condition)
result.notes:
All fields check out. arXiv 2406.00257 (v1 1 Jun 2024, v2 4 Oct 2024). Published in Findings of EMNLP 2024, pp. 3334-3368, ACL Anthology ID 2024.findings-emnlp.191 (https://aclanthology.org/2024.findings-emnlp.191/). The Anthology version drops the subtitle; its title is just "Are Large Vision Language Models up to the Challenge of Chart Comprehension and Reasoning". The abstracts differ: arXiv v1 says GPT-4V and Gemini on four tasks, while the Anthology says closed and open-source LVLMs on five tasks. Models in the v2 body: GPT-4V, Gemini, Claude-3-haiku, Phi-3-vision, plus the MatCha and UniChart baselines.

The first half of the candidate's key finding matches the abstract. The ChartQA* numbers are not in the abstract, but I checked them in the arXiv v2 HTML body (Table 6): GPT-4V drops from 57.51 to 20.52 (-36.99) and Gemini from 52.04 to 38.53 (-13.51) when data-value labels are removed. The paper says both models get worse without the labels and GPT-4V is hit harder. It also notes that GPT-4V often declines to answer when labels are missing. So part of GPT-4V's drop comes from refusals, not wrong readings, which matters when comparing this to our no-numbers condition. The relevance tag is right: this paper has ChartQA* (equivalent to our no-numbers condition) but nothing like our consistent-vs-conflicting labels condition.

result.title: Protecting multimodal large language models against misleading visualizations
result.authors: Jonathan Tonglet, Tinne Tuytelaars, Marie-Francine Moens, Iryna Gurevych
result.venue: ACL 2026 (Proceedings of the 64th Annual Meeting of the ACL, Volume 1: Long Papers), pp. 8329-8349
result.key_finding: On misleading visualizations (charts that distort the underlying data), MLLM question-answering accuracy drops on average to the random-baseline level; of six inference-time methods compared, table-based QA and redrawing the visualization are effective, improving accuracy by up to 19.6 percentage points.
result.what_it_measures: MLLM QA accuracy on charts that distort the data with misleaders such as truncated, inverted and dual axes or inconsistent tick intervals (list from the arXiv paper body), and six inference-time mitigations.
result.relevance: partial overlap (inverted axis and odd ticks are text-vs-geometry conflicts close to our conflict edits, but they are framed as charts misleading humans, not as a clean marks-vs-text test with a matched consistent version)
result.notes: Existence, title, first author, year, venue and URL all check out on the ACL Anthology page (arXiv preprint 2502.20503, first posted Feb 2025). The candidate key finding goes slightly too far. The abstract gives "without compromising accuracy on non-misleading ones" as the goal of the comparison, not as a result for both methods. The arXiv body (v4) says table-based QA lowers accuracy on non-misleading charts by up to 8.5 pp, and only redrawing shows no significant drop. So "without hurting accuracy on normal charts" holds for redrawing only. "Converting the chart to a table" is also loose: the method is table-based QA, which extracts the data table and answers from it. what_it_measures is accurate. The body lists 17 misleader types, including inverted axis, truncated axis, inappropriate axis range, inconsistent tick intervals, dual axis, 3D effects and misleading annotations. The evaluation data are CALVI, CHARTOM, VLAT, a new real-world set of 42 misleading charts, and 2,500 ChartQA charts as non-misleading controls. The six methods are: a misleader warning in the prompt, extracted axes, extracted table, axes plus table, table-based QA, and redrawing via code generation. The relevance note holds: it is not a matched consistent-vs-conflict marks/text test. One caution: web search summaries tie this paper to Misviz (2,604 real charts) and Misviz-synth (81,814 charts). Those come from a separate Tonglet et al. paper, not this one, so do not cite them as from this paper.

result.title: ChartBench: A Benchmark for Complex Visual Reasoning in Charts
result.authors: Zhengzhuo Xu, Sinan Du, Yiyan Qi, Chengjin Xu, Chun Yuan, Jian Guo
result.key_finding: ChartBench (42 categories, 66.6k charts, 600k QA pairs, many charts without data-point annotations, scored with a new Acc+ metric) shows in tests of 18 open-source and 3 proprietary MLLMs that they are limited at chart comprehension, and the authors add chain-of-thought and supervised fine-tuning baselines to improve results on unannotated charts.
result.what_it_measures: Chart comprehension on 66.6k charts across 42 chart types (600k QA pairs). Many of the charts have no data-point annotations, so the model has to derive values from color, legends and the coordinate system. It reports annotated and unannotated accuracy separately and uses an Acc+ metric.
result.relevance: Same question, matching our consistent vs no-numbers contrast. The paper body says the annotated-minus-unannotated gap grows as models get stronger (e.g. GPT-4V about +34 pts): stronger models gain more from reading printed numbers than from reading the marks. It has no conflict condition.
result.notes: The arXiv abstract page confirms the title and all six authors (first author Zhengzhuo Xu). v1 is dated 26 Dec 2023, v2 29 Jan 2024 and v3 19 Jun 2024, so 2023 is correct. The venue is arXiv: the abstract page has no journal-ref, and the official GitHub README (IDEA-FinAI/ChartBench) cites it as "journal={ArXiv}, volume={abs/2312.15915}". I found no peer-reviewed acceptance. ChartMoE, a related paper by the same first author, is ICLR 2025; that is not this paper. The candidate key finding matches the abstract. I also checked the relevance claim in the paper body (arXiv HTML v3, Table 6). The paper says the annotated-vs-unannotated gap "widens significantly" as MLLMs get stronger, e.g. InternLM-XComposer-v2 +18.36% and GPT-4V +34.40% (GPT-4V scores 77.40% annotated vs 43.00% unannotated). The +34 figure is correct. One caveat: search snippets of the v1/v2 abstract give 2.1K charts / 16.8K QA pairs. The 66.6k / 600k figures are from v3, so cite v3 numbers alongside v3.

result.title: Do MLLMs Really Understand the Charts?
result.authors: Xiao Zhang, Dongyuan Li, Liuyu Xiang, Yao Zhang, Cheng Zhong, Zhaofeng He
result.key_finding: Most MLLMs show alarming hallucinations and a significant drop in performance on charts without annotations. The authors argue this is because the models rely on visual recognition rather than visual reasoning, and they introduce ChartVRBench, which tests value estimation on non-annotated charts, along with ChartVR-3B/7B models trained with VR-RFT that beat strong proprietary models on it and generalize to other chart benchmarks.
result.what_it_measures: ChartVRBench: estimating the numerical value of a queried data point on non-annotated charts, so text shortcuts are removed and only visual reasoning is tested. It also trains ChartVR-3B/7B models with visual-reasoning RL fine-tuning.
result.relevance: Same question, for our no-numbers condition. The paper body reports GPT-4o at about 21% on ChartVRBench against about 88% for humans. Like ChartBench, it removes text but never makes text contradict the marks.
result.notes: Checked against the arXiv abstract page (v1 27 Aug 2025, v2 15 Dec 2025, cs.CL) and the v2 HTML body. Title, first author (Xiao Zhang), year 2025 and URL are correct. There is no comments field or note of acceptance anywhere, so the venue is plain "arXiv". The candidate's "v2 Dec 2025" detail is right but doesn't belong in the venue field. The candidate's key finding is basically faithful, with one fix: the abstract hedges the cause with "We argue", while the candidate states "because they rely largely on visual recognition" as established fact. The rewrite keeps the hedge and adds the paper's main result, ChartVR beating proprietary models. Relevance claims I checked in the body: Table 2 gives GPT-4o 20.87% overall and humans 87.57%, so "about 21% vs about 88%" is correct. The task is a numerical answer from a chart image plus question, where the values do not appear as text labels. The paper never builds charts where printed numbers contradict the marks, so the "removes text but never makes it contradict" point is accurate. Sources: https://arxiv.org/abs/2509.04457 and https://arxiv.org/html/2509.04457v2

result.title: Towards Understanding Graphical Perception in Large Multimodal Models
result.authors: Kai Zhang, Jianwei Yang, Jeevana Priya Inala, Chandan Singh, Jianfeng Gao, Yu Su, Chenglong Wang (Microsoft Research / Ohio State University)
result.key_finding: The authors used graphical-perception theory to build an automated framework for testing chart perception in LMMs, and found that leading models including GPT-4o fail to generalize across chart types, fail to understand basic visual elements, and fail to cross-reference values within a chart.
result.what_it_measures: An evaluation framework built on graphical-perception theory that tests LMMs across chart types, visual elements and task variants. It includes bar charts with and without value annotations, plus pixel-level attention analysis.
result.relevance: Same question (reliance on annotations). The paper body reports GPT-4o drops from 85.0% on annotated bars to 53.4% without annotations. Without labels, models still find the right region but cannot read the value off the axis. This is the attention-level version of what our no-numbers condition measures.
result.notes:
All fields check out against the arXiv abs page. Title matches exactly. First author is Kai Zhang. It was submitted 13 Mar 2025 and only v1 exists. The comments field reads "Work in Progress" and there is no journal-ref. Two searches turned up no peer-reviewed venue, so the venue stays arXiv. The candidate key_finding repeats the abstract's three shortcomings nearly word for word, so it is faithful. I only added the framing (built on graphical-perception theory, automated evaluation, GPT-4o among the models tested).

I checked the relevance claims against the HTML full text (arxiv.org/html/2503.10857v1) and they hold up:
(a) Table 3 gives GPT-4o 85.0% on bar charts with annotations and 53.4% without. That is a 31.6-point drop on bars, and the paper says GPT-4o's average drop across chart types is 31.8%.
(b) Section 5 (RQ3) has a pixel-level attention analysis. It finds that models usually locate the right region, but they read the value from it imprecisely and give only approximate answers. Note that this attention result is not in the abstract, so cite it to the paper body (Sec. 5 / Table 3).

Caveat: this is a different paper from "Evaluating Graphical Perception with Multimodal LLMs" (arXiv 2504.04221), which shows up next to it in searches. Don't mix them up when citing.

result.title: Evaluating Graphical Perception with Multimodal LLMs
result.authors: Rami Huu Nguyen, Kenichi Maeda, Mahsa Geshvadi, Daniel Haehn (UMass Boston)
result.venue: IEEE PacificVis 2025 (arXiv comments field: "IEEE Pacific Visualization 2025 Conference"; arXiv 2504.04221)
result.key_finding: Reproducing Cleveland and McGill's 1984 graphical-perception experiment with fine-tuned and pretrained MLLMs under zero-shot prompting, the authors find that MLLMs outperform human task performance in some cases but not in others.
result.what_it_measures: A reproduction of Cleveland & McGill's 1984 graphical-perception experiment (value judgments in pie and bar charts) on fine-tuned, pretrained and zero-shot MLLMs, compared with human error.
result.relevance: Background. Classic marks-only perception (angle vs length vs position) with no printed numbers. Useful for justifying why our marks include needle angle, slice size and bar height, and for the expectation that angle/area are harder than position/length.
result.notes:
I checked this on the arXiv abstract page. Submitted 5 Apr 2025 (v1). There is no journal-ref. The only venue evidence is the comments field, and I found no IEEE Xplore entry, so cite it as "PacificVis 2025 (per arXiv)". The candidate's key finding is a near-verbatim quote from the abstract, so it is faithful. I only added the setup (fine-tuned plus pretrained models, zero-shot) to the sentence.

Correction to what_it_measures: according to the paper body (read through a summarizer, not checked line by line), it runs more than pie vs bar. There are five Cleveland-McGill experiments: (E1) elementary perceptual tasks (position, length, direction, angle, area, volume, curvature, shading), (E2) position-angle (pie vs bar), (E3) position-length (grouped vs divided bars), (E4) bars vs framed rectangles, and (E5) point clouds / Weber's law.

Models tested: GPT-4o, Gemini 1.5 Flash, Gemini 1.0 Pro Vision, Llama 3.2-Vision 11B, plus fine-tuned Llama 3.2-Vision variants.

Results from the body (same caveat): MLLMs predict values more accurately from bar charts than from pie charts. This supports the relevance note that angle is harder than position/length. On several tasks (e.g. E2 bars, E3) the models reach lower MLAE than the human baselines. So for the blog, do not say "MLLMs are worse than humans at charts." The honest framing is "better on some tasks, worse on others."

Relevance as a benchmark: all charts are marks-only, with no printed numbers. It measures pure visual value regression. It does not test any text-vs-marks conflict, so it is background, not a direct precedent for the cue-conflict experiment.

result.title: Inside VLM Chart Reading: Tracing Value Reading from Vertical Bar Charts Across Space and Depth
result.authors: Tianhao Niu, Qingfu Zhu, Wanxiang Che
result.key_finding: Using counterfactual activation patching in Qwen2.5-VL-7B-Instruct and InternVL3.5-8B, the authors find three things: the changed bar-top region restores much more answer preference than the unchanged bar body even though it has fewer visual tokens; legend and series states stop being locally recoverable at earlier layers than bar-geometry and axis-scale states, and that information moves from legend image regions to prompt-series positions in the middle layers; and both models can combine geometry and scale states taken from separate donor charts to favor the combined target, with Qwen less able to do this than InternVL.
result.what_it_measures: A mechanistic study using counterfactual activation patching on Qwen2.5-VL-7B and InternVL3.5-8B reading values from vertical bar charts. One counterfactual multiplies all y-axis tick values by 2 while keeping the bar geometry pixel-fixed. A factorial analysis tests whether bar geometry and axis scale taken from different charts get recombined.
result.relevance: Partial overlap, and the closest stimulus design to ours: tick text changes while the marks stay fixed, as in our relabeled and inverted-axis conflicts. Differences: no value labels on the bars, internal patching instead of a behavioral marks-vs-text tally, and different models (not PaliGemma), English only.
result.notes:
I opened the abstract and the arXiv HTML version. The paper exists, submitted 12 Sep 2026 (v1). Authors are Tianhao Niu, Qingfu Zhu and Wanxiang Che, so the first author is correct. No journal-ref or acceptance is listed, so the venue stays arXiv. Title, year and URL are correct.

Problem with the candidate key finding: the first half (bar-top beats bar body despite fewer tokens) matches the abstract word for word. The second half, "route geometry and axis-scale information through distinct pathways across layers", is NOT in the paper. The abstract's layer-wise result is about legend and series states being lost earlier than geometry and scale states, plus a legend-to-prompt-series handoff. The factorial result shows the two factors can be recombined downstream. It is not evidence of separate routes; the HTML body says so explicitly.

what_it_measures is accurate. Table 1 has the axis-scale counterfactual: multiply all y-axis tick values and the target value by 2 while keeping the rendered bar geometry. The synthetic charts have no value labels on the bars.

Factorial numbers from the body: InternVL R = 0.977 whether the states come from separate donors or one image; Qwen R = 0.803 with separate donors vs 0.867 with one image. The authors call this higher context sensitivity in Qwen.

The candidate's relevance note holds up: the stimulus design is close to ours, but the study patches internal activations rather than counting marks-vs-text answers, uses no PaliGemma, and is English only.

result.title: ChartInsights: Evaluating Multimodal Large Language Models for Low-Level Chart Question Answering
result.authors: Yifan Wu, Lutao Yan, Leixian Shen, Yunhai Wang, Nan Tang, Yuyu Luo
result.key_finding: Across 19 MLLMs on 22,347 low-level chart QA samples (10 tasks, 7 chart types), average accuracy is 39.8% with GPT-4o best at 69.17%; the proposed Chain-of-Charts text prompt raises GPT-4o to 83.58% (+14.41%), and adding a visual prompt that points to the relevant chart elements raises it to 84.32%.
result.what_it_measures: Low-level chart QA (22,347 samples, 10 analysis tasks, 7 chart types, 19 MLLMs), plus a chart-variation experiment that alters visual elements: data labels enlarged, shrunk or removed, colors changed, noise added.
result.relevance: Partial overlap, through the label-removal variants. The paper body reports that removing data labels hurts GPT-4o across seven chart types, but improves anomaly detection (+17.5%) and filtering (+5.5%). So printed numbers can pull a model away from comparing marks, which our conflict condition tests directly.
result.notes: I checked the arXiv abstract page (v1 11 May 2024, v4 6 Nov 2024; the comment just says "EMNLP 2024 Conference Paper") and the ACL Anthology page, which lists it in Findings of the ACL: EMNLP 2024, pp. 12174-12200, DOI 10.18653/v1/2024.findings-emnlp.710. The paper exists and the title is correct. It is arXiv 2608.17205, v1 only (submitted 17 Aug 2026), with the comment "20 pages. Under review". result.what_it_measures: Converts benchmark charts into executable code, checks the reconstruction, generates counterfactual variants with changed underlying data, and recomputes the gold answers, so that models are tested on whether they update their answer when the chart changes.
result.relevance: Partial overlap. A chart-specific counterfactual benchmark testing whether models really read the chart or pattern-match. It changes the data (marks and text together), whereas we keep the marks fixed and change only the text.
result.notes: I checked the arXiv abstract page (v1 26 May 2026, v2 6 Sep 2026). Title, all four authors (first author Yifan Jiang), year and URL match. The arXiv comments field says "Accepted at EMNLP 2026 Main", so the venue is EMNLP 2026 Main and the arXiv ID is 2605.27311. The candidate key finding matches the abstract. My rewrite only adds what "counterfactual" means here and uses the abstract's wording, "novel visual reasoning pathways". The candidate's what_it_measures field also matches the abstract: the pipeline turns charts into executable code, checks that the reconstruction is faithful, generates variants and recomputes answers from executable QA logic, and the paper measures variant sensitivity and generalizability. The relevance note holds: this paper changes the underlying data, so the marks and the text change together, while our experiment keeps the marks fixed and changes only the text.

result.title: Vision language models are blind: Failing to translate detailed visual features into words
result.authors: Pooyan Rahmanzadehgervi et al. (Logan Bolton, Mohammad Reza Taesiri, Anh Totti Nguyen)
result.key_finding: On BlindTest, 7 very simple low-level tasks such as checking whether two circles overlap or counting line intersections, four state-of-the-art VLMs average only 58.07% (best: Claude 3.5 Sonnet at 77.84%, against an expected 100% for humans); they struggle most when shapes overlap or sit close together and reach near 100% when the shapes are spaced apart, and linear probes show the vision encoder holds enough information while the language model fails to decode it into correct answers.
result.what_it_measures: BlindTest: 7 trivially simple low-level geometric tasks (e.g. whether two circles overlap, counting line intersections, which letter is circled) that need precise reading of shapes rather than text.
result.relevance: Background. It explains why reading bar heights, slice sizes or needle angles without printed numbers (our no-numbers condition) is hard for VLMs, and why they may fall back on text when it is present.
result.notes: Checked against the arXiv abstract page (v1 9 Jul 2024, current v6 27 Mar 2025) and the CVF open-access page for ACCV 2024 (Proceedings of ACCV 2024, pp. 18-34). All fields are correct. The ACCV proceedings version uses the short title "Vision language models are blind"; the subtitle "Failing to translate detailed visual features into words" appears only on the later arXiv v6. The arXiv page has no journal-ref field. The candidate key finding is accurate. Small precision points: the 58.07% average covers four specific state-of-the-art VLMs, not VLMs in general. The rewrite also adds two findings from the abstract: models do much worse when primitives overlap or sit close together, and score near 100% once the shapes are spaced apart. The relevance note (background for the no-numbers condition) is reasonable but is our interpretation; the paper does not test charts directly. The authors do mention real-world failures such as telling whether a stock price crosses a threshold line.
